concept.body: The whole construction rides on equidistance. Q is drawn by two arcs of the SAME radius from A and from B, so QA = QB. Any point equally far from A and B sits on the perpendicular bisector of AB — and since P is AB's midpoint, line PQ is that bisector, crossing at 90°.

explanationVariants: Equal-radius arcs from A and B force QA = QB, placing Q on AB's perpendicular bisector.
The same compass opening from both endpoints is exactly what makes Q equidistant.

widget.prompt: In the construction, why does point Q lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB?

options.label: Equal-radius arcs from A and B make QA = QB
options.feedback: Equidistance from the two endpoints is the defining property of the perpendicular bisector.

options.label: Q is the highest point of the arcs
options.feedback: "Highest" isn't a geometric property — Q's role comes from being EQUALLY far from A and B, whatever its height.

options.label: Q is twice as far from A as from B
options.feedback: The arcs use the SAME radius, so QA = QB — equal, not double. Equal distances put Q on the bisector.

options.label: A and B were placed by eye
options.feedback: A and B come from one compass swing about P, so PA = PB exactly — nothing is by eye.

steps.body: The perpendicular-bisector trick has a cousin. To raise a **perpendicular at a point P that lies ON a line**, first make P the midpoint of a little segment, then bisect it. Two compass openings, and a clean 90° rises from P — no protractor, no guessing.

predict.prompt: P sits ON the line. The construction first marks two points equidistant from P, then swings equal arcs from those. Why does that force a RIGHT angle at P?

options.label: The crossings are equidistant from both marks, so the line through them is the perpendicular bisector of the segment they span — and P is its midpoint
It doesn't force it — you line it up by eye and check
Any line drawn through two arc crossings is automatically perpendicular

predict.reveal: The two marks are equal distances from P, so P is the MIDPOINT of the segment joining them. The crossings are equidistant from both marks, which is the definition of the perpendicular bisector of that segment — and a perpendicular bisector meets the segment square, at its midpoint, which is P.

widget.prompt: Construct the perpendicular to the line at point P (P is on the line). Reveal each stage.

panels.title: Mark equal distances
panels.body: Put the compass point on P. Swing one opening to cut the line on BOTH sides, marking A and B. Now PA = PB — P is the midpoint of AB.

panels.title: Widen and arc from A
panels.body: Open WIDER than PA. With the point on A, swing an arc above the line.

panels.title: Same-radius arc from B
panels.body: Keep that opening. Arc from B; it crosses the first arc at Q.

panels.title: Draw PQ
panels.body: The straightedge line through P and Q is perpendicular to the original line at P.

widget.continueFeedback: Reveal each compass move in order.
widget.successFeedback: Line PQ meets the original line at P at a perfect right angle.

widget.prompt: The two marks either side of P are 8 apart. Open the compass until the arcs from them cross — find the smallest whole radius that does it.
widget.successFeedback: Radius 5 — the first whole opening that clears half of 8. The two marks are equal distances from P, so P is the MIDPOINT between them; the crossings are equidistant from both marks, which is the perpendicular bisector of that segment. A perpendicular bisector meets the segment square, at its midpoint — and its midpoint is P.
widget.lowFeedback: The arcs from the two marks do not yet cross. Together they must span more than the 8 between them — the radius has to clear 4.
widget.highFeedback: They do cross, but you were asked for the SMALLEST whole radius that reaches. Ease back down until they are just about to come apart.

predict.prompt: P sits ON the line, with two marks stepped off equally either side of it. Where must the crossings of two equal arcs from those marks lie?

options.label: Directly above and below P — nowhere else is equidistant from both marks
Nearer whichever mark the compass was opened from first
Anywhere the arcs happen to meet; the position is not fixed

predict.reveal: Directly above and below P. Equal arcs from two marks meet only on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them — and because the marks were stepped off equally from P, that bisector passes through P itself.

steps.body: Why is it a right angle?
explanationVariants: Q is equidistant from A and B (same-radius arcs), and so is P (it's the midpoint). Two points equidistant from A and B determine the perpendicular bisector of AB — which passes through P at 90°.
PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB: every point on it is equally far from A and B, and it crosses AB squarely at the midpoint P.

widget.prompt: What guarantees PQ ⊥ the line, without measuring?

options.label: Both P and Q are equidistant from A and B, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB
options.feedback: Two points equally far from A and B pin down AB's perpendicular bisector — and it meets AB at 90° through the midpoint P.

options.label: Q was drawn directly above P by eye
options.feedback: Nothing was placed by eye — Q is fixed by two equal-radius arcs. Its being on the perpendicular follows from equidistance, not from looking straight.

options.label: The compass always makes right angles
options.feedback: A compass makes CIRCLES, not right angles. The 90° comes from the equidistance argument, not the tool itself.

options.label: Because PA = PB, angle APQ must be 90°
options.feedback: PA = PB only makes P the midpoint — it doesn't force the angle. The second pair of equal arcs (giving Q) is what squares the corner.

steps.body: One perpendicular, two right angles. Because the original line is straight, the perpendicular splits the straight angle at P into two equal parts. Each must be **half of 180°** — so raising a perpendicular is really the same move as bisecting a straight angle.

explanationVariants: The line is a straight angle, 180°, and the perpendicular bisects it: 180 ÷ 2 = 90° on each side.
Two equal angles that fill a straight line must each be 90°.

widget.prompt: The perpendicular at P splits the straight line into two equal angles. How many degrees is each?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is the WHOLE straight angle. The perpendicular cuts it into two equal pieces: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°.
45° would be a quarter of the straight angle — but a perpendicular makes HALVES: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°.

explanationVariants: Raising a perpendicular at P bisects the straight angle (180°) at P — same compass logic as bisecting any angle.
The line through P is a 180° angle; the perpendicular is its bisector, so this IS an angle-bisector construction in disguise.

widget.prompt: Raising a perpendicular at a point on a line is secretly the same as…

options.label: bisecting the straight angle at that point
options.feedback: The line is a 180° angle at P; the perpendicular splits it into two 90° halves — an angle bisection.

options.label: copying a segment
options.feedback: Copying a segment reproduces a LENGTH elsewhere — no angle is created. Here we're halving an angle, not moving a length.

options.label: constructing an equilateral triangle
options.feedback: That construction builds three 60° angles from equal radii. A perpendicular makes 90°, by halving a straight angle.

options.label: finding a midpoint only
options.feedback: The midpoint of AB is just step one. The right angle needs the second pair of arcs — the bisection of the straight angle.

hints: What angle does each perpendicular make with the shared line?
Both make 90° with the same straight line — on the same side.
Two lines both perpendicular to a third: compare their directions.
explanationVariants: Each perpendicular makes 90° with the shared line, so they make 0° with EACH OTHER — same direction. Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
In a plane, if line a ⊥ c and line b ⊥ c, then a ∥ b — both are tilted exactly 90° off c, hence identically tilted.

widget.prompt: You raise a perpendicular to line ℓ at point P, and another perpendicular to ℓ at a different point R. How are the two perpendiculars related?

options.label: They are parallel to each other
options.feedback: Both stand at 90° to the same line ℓ, so they point the same way — in a plane, that makes them parallel.

options.label: They intersect at one point above ℓ
options.feedback: Two lines equally perpendicular to ℓ never tilt toward each other — no meeting point. They stay parallel.

options.label: They are perpendicular to each other
options.feedback: Each is perpendicular to ℓ, not to the other. Sharing a perpendicular direction makes them PARALLEL, not mutually perpendicular.

options.label: It depends on how far apart P and R are
options.feedback: Distance doesn't tilt them — both are locked at 90° to ℓ regardless of spacing, so they're always parallel.

takeaways: Perpendicular at P: mark equal PA = PB, then arc equal radii from A and B to get Q.
It works because P and Q are both equidistant from A and B — the perpendicular-bisector logic.
It's really bisecting the 180° straight angle: two 90° halves.
steps.teaser: Next: drop a perpendicular FROM a point that floats off the line — the shortest path down.
